messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Chef
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Violence: Violence, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds, Loss of Control: Lack of control
  Maladaptive Strategies: Revenge Fantasies: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening, Hopelessness: I have no future

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi is a 21-year-old Ghanaian-American man who works as a line chef at a busy downtown restaurant. He presented for treatment approximately four months after being sexually assaulted by an acquaintance at a gathering he attended after a late shift. The assault occurred in a back room while music played loudly elsewhere in the apartment; at one point a car alarm outside cut through the noise, and Kofi remembers the sound clearly because it was the moment he understood he could not get away. He could not move freely, could not call out without consequence, and that absolute loss of physical agency became the defining texture of the experience.

In the weeks that followed, Kofi found that ordinary sounds in the kitchen — the sharp clatter of a pan, a colleague shouting an order, and most acutely the rumble and beep of delivery trucks in the alley behind the restaurant — could pull the full memory back without warning, as though no time had passed at all. When the memory arrived it came with sound: he would hear, internally and vividly, the car alarm from that night, and the voices, and the specific quality of his own silence. He could not explain this to his supervisor when asked why he had frozen mid-service; he would begin to describe what happened and lose the thread entirely, the words dissolving before he could finish. Those intrusive returns of the memory, in turn, reliably reactivated his sense that danger was present right now, and he would scan the kitchen for threats — tracking the movements of colleagues, tensing whenever someone crossed behind him quickly — as if the assault were still in progress.

That persistent sense of threat had become structural in his life. Sudden movements by anyone nearby put him on guard immediately, and he felt no relief even at home, remaining watchful in his own apartment in ways that exhausted him. The threat state fed back into the memory directly: when his body was already primed and scanning, the threshold for a full intrusion dropped, and sounds that might otherwise pass unnoticed — a car outside, a raised voice through the wall — were enough to trigger the complete recollection again. To manage this, Kofi had developed several strategies that felt necessary even when he recognised they were not helping. He monitored his body constantly, checking for signs of injury or physiological alarm as though verifying he was still intact. He detached himself from the memories when they surfaced, pushing them away before they could fully form. And in quieter moments, particularly at night, he found himself constructing elaborate revenge fantasies about the person responsible — replaying scenarios in which he had power and the outcome was different.

These strategies, however, had begun to reinforce the very difficulties they were meant to contain. The detachment prevented any coherent processing of what had happened, so the memories remained fragmented, easily triggered, and loaded with the same raw intensity as the night itself. The body monitoring kept his attention fixed on internal threat signals, which meant the threshold for false alarms stayed low, and he continued to react as though danger were imminent in situations that were objectively safe. The revenge fantasies, rather than relieving distress, circled back into his appraisals of the event — because imagining what he should have done implied, to Kofi, that he had failed to do it. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt unshakeable, that someone else in his position would have stopped it. He felt that he had acted in ways that violated who he understood himself to be, though he struggled to articulate exactly what he meant by this, only that something essential had been compromised. These beliefs, in turn, made the memories harder to bear when they surfaced, amplifying their emotional charge, and they lowered his tolerance for any reminder — so that even the minor associations of daily life, a car sound, a moment of feeling constrained during a busy service, could become intolerable. He had no sense of a future he was moving toward. That hopelessness sat separately from everything else, a flat and quiet certainty that had settled over him.

What finally brought Kofi to seek help was a service incident in which he walked off the line mid-shift after a delivery truck idled in the alley for several minutes. He was given a formal warning. He came to the first session saying he did not expect therapy to change anything, but that he needed, at minimum, to be able to finish a shift.
